# Anonymous Submissions store no person and no time, and are unlinkable at rest, not against a restore

**Threat model.** The Lead, Organization admins, and anyone using the product (UI, API, exports) must never be able to link a member to their Submission, and neither can an operator reading stored data, dumps, or R2 backups. We do **not** claim to defend against an operator who restores the Durable Object to a past moment (point-in-time recovery replays every write, including the one transaction that writes a Participation record and its Submission), reads Cloudflare's internal edge logs, or changes the code to start logging. Against that we use controls instead: only named people can trigger a restore, the privacy page states the 30-day restore window, and code changes on the submission path need review. The answer page's "Your name is never stored with your answers" is true of everything stored.

**Design.**
- Everything lives in the Organization's Durable Object. There is no per-Round object. The first Answer writes the Participation record and a Submission holding that one Answer in **one transaction**, which is how a double submission is rejected (a unique Participation record per Round and Person).
- An anonymous Submission stores only its Round, its Answers, and an Edit key hash. It stores **no person, no Invitation, and no time at all**, not even the day SPEC allows. A Participation record stores Round, Person, and the fact of answering, also with no time.
- Submission and Answer tables are `WITHOUT ROWID` with random 128-bit keys. Reads aggregate or sort by the random key. Dumps and backups are written in key order.
- **The anonymous Submission table has no person column, ever.** Attributed Submissions get their own table, so no bug can put a name on an anonymous answer.
- The Invitation token travels in the **URL fragment**, so the answer page GET (and every link scanner) never sends it. The page POSTs it to a **separate Submission Worker** with logs, traces, tail, Logpush, and Analytics Engine writes all off. That Worker logs error codes only. Tokens are stored only as hashes.
- The **browser generates the Edit key** and sends only its SHA-256 hash with the first Answer. Later Answers and changes carry only the Edit key. **No request may carry both an Invitation token and an Edit key**, and the server rejects one that does.

## Considered Options

- **Submissions in a separate Durable Object.** Rejected: without one transaction, a crash either loses the Answer or allows a second Submission, and the timing gap still exists.
- **Shuffled batch writes.** Rejected: buffered Answers are lost if the object is evicted, and it defends only against the restore threat we don't claim to cover.
- **A nullable person column shared with attributed mode.** Rejected: a single bug would put names on anonymous answers.

## Consequences

Response and answer counts come from Participation records. Answer latency is measured only in tests on a preview stage. Deleting a Person deletes their Participation records, and their anonymous Submissions survive. A member who loses the Edit key cannot change their answers, and that is accepted.
3:SPEC §5.1 said each rating link in an email "records the answer". Email security scanners (Microsoft Defender runs headless Chrome) fetch every link, so recording on GET would count scanners as voters. Some scanners can also produce trusted events, so saving on any interaction would still be unsafe. A rating link (`/a#t=<token>&v=<1–5>`) therefore opens the answer page with that value preselected and writes nothing. The answer is saved only when the member taps "Save and continue", which sits directly under the anonymity statement, or changes the value. A member who taps in the email and leaves without touching the page loses that answer. We accept that loss as the price of never counting a scanner.
7:- The token exchange that loads the page has no side effects, so R1 has no open tracking at all.
132:- A member can change answers until the round closes. In anonymous rounds this needs a design that does not link the person to the submission on the server. The recommended approach is a random edit key that only the member's browser stores. If the member loses the key, they cannot edit, and that is acceptable.
134:- A member has a private history page that shows their own past attributed answers. It also shows their anonymous answers if their browser still holds those edit keys. Nobody else can see this page.

<result>I found no blockers. The gate in `SubmissionRoutes.ts` is correct, and the real answer page still works. The weaknesses are in the tests.

I ran the privacy file (75 tests) and `SubmissionWorker.test.ts` (2 tests). Both pass.

**Checked, no bypass:**
- **Query params:** `searchParams.has` covers duplicate params and percent-encoded names. Case variants such as `Token` or `EDITKEY` are never read, so they are harmless.
- **Headers:** Effect request headers are lowercase, and the server no longer reads them anyway.
- **Stored hash:** `/answer` refuses `editKeyHash`, and `/exchange` refuses it too. `/first-answer` accepts a hash only together with a valid token, and records it via `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. A hash on its own edits nothing.
- **Schema decode:** a body whose fields fail to decode becomes `{}`, which still ends in a 400.
- **Answer page:**
  - `main.ts` posts `{token}` to `/exchange`, `{token, editKeyHash}` to `/first-answer` and `{editKey, ...}` to `/answer`, all with only a content-type header.
  - `sha256Hex` emits lowercase hex padded to 64 characters, so it matches `/^[0-9a-f]{64}$/`.
  - The CORS allow-headers list was narrowed to `Content-Type`, which is compatible.

**Findings (all MINOR, all in `packages/cloudflare/src/SubmissionRoutes.privacy.test.ts`):**

1. **Body refusal cases that pass without the gate (lines ~264-305).**
   - `/answer` "body editKeyHash of the Edit key", `/answer` "body edit_key_hash" and `/answer` "body token" send no `editKey`. Without the new `/answer` gates they would still return 400 "Missing edit key".
   - `/first-answer` "token with edit_key_hash" returns 400 "Missing edit key hash" even with no gate.
   - Fix: give the `/answer` cases a valid `editKey` where the gate is the only thing that can refuse. For `editKeyHash`, send `{editKey: EDIT_KEY, editKeyHash}`. For the token case, the existing A5 test already covers token plus `editKey`, so `{token}` alone cannot prove the `/answer` token gate and that case can be dropped.
   - The `/exchange` `editKeyHash` and `/first-answer` malformed-hash cases do prove their gates.
2. **No A5 case on the routes in this file.**
   - The issue asks for the same refusal on every route. A5 (`{token, editKey}` → 400, no Organization call) is only tested in `SubmissionWorker.test.ts:79`.
   - Fix: add `{token, editKey}` bodies for `/exchange`, `/first-answer` and `/answer` to `bodyRefusals`, and assert `calls` is empty.
3. **The `/my-answers` test assertion is looser.**
   - It now accepts any 4xx instead of a 404, because query and header credentials give 400 before routing.

content.text:
PR #133 is open and its checks are still running, so it is not merged yet. One part of the brief wasn't followed: `/first-answer` still accepts the Edit key hash, because ADR 0005 requires it.

- **What the answer page sends:** credentials only in POST bodies, never in the URL query or headers. `/exchange` gets `{token}`, `/first-answer` gets `{token, editKeyHash}` (hashed in the browser), and `/answer` gets `{editKey}`. So the page didn't need to change.
- **Why the hash stays on `/first-answer`:** ADR 0005 says the browser sends only the hash with the first Answer, and that no request may carry the token and the Edit key together. Taking the raw key there would break that rule (invariant A5), which would need a new ADR. The issue's attack, editing answers with the hash stored in D1 alone, only worked on `/answer`, and that is closed. On `/first-answer` the hash now needs a valid token and must be 64 lowercase hex characters. If you still want the raw key there, it needs a new ADR that changes A5.
- **What changed** (`packages/cloudflare/src/SubmissionRoutes.ts`):
  - A token or Edit key (or hash) in the query string or in the `x-invitation-token`/`x-edit-key` headers gets a 400 before D1 or any Organization is touched.
  - `/answer` takes only the raw Edit key and hashes it on the server; a hash or a token there gets a 400.
  - `/exchange` refuses a hash.
  - `edit_key` and `edit_key_hash` are gone from the body schema, and the two credential headers are gone from the CORS allow-list.
- **Tests:** `SubmissionRoutes.privacy.test.ts` now checks every query, header, body-hash and A5 case on all three routes: each gets a 400 with no Organization call, and the valid body paths still work.
- **Reviewer:** found no bypass. It flagged weak test cases, and I fixed three: two cases passed without the new checks, A5 wasn't tested on these routes, and uppercase hex wasn't tested. The `/my-answers` test now accepts any 4xx instead of exactly 404; I left that as is.
- **Checks run:** typecheck, typecheck:effect, lint, format:check, `pnpm test` (881 passed), `pnpm test:privacy` (209 passed before the extra cases; that file then ran alone with 79 passing), and the web build plus budget test all pass. The Submission Worker has no workerd adapter test, so I ran `SubmissionWorker.test.ts` alone instead (passes). The e2e answer test wasn't run, since it needs a deployed stage; the page is unchanged.
- **Not merged:** I didn't watch the checks with `--watch` because this environment doesn't allow it. The first push hit a GitHub 500, and the retry worked.
